t: Today we're digging into a piece that lit up both sides of the Pacific this week. ChinaTalk's Irene Zhang, in her essay How Chinese AI Radicalizes, asks a question nobody in AI safety is comfortable with: what happens when China's youngest AI researchers stop listening to American warnings entirely?
And this isn't about Beijing's official line. It's about the technologists themselves. The story starts inside DeepSeek, with a researcher named Liu Shengyu.

Right. On September thirteenth, right after DeepSeek released V point four point one Flash, Liu wrote a personal blog post that went viral. His framing: as AI develops, society trends toward one of two extremes. Communism, or Cyberpunk twenty seventy-seven.

Which is a pretty striking way to put it. Either the productive forces get liberated and everyone's living standard rises, or a few tech companies hoard the frontier, and a tiny minority achieves what he calls machine ascension, while everyone else makes do with, quote, feeble AI.
And he immediately jokes, let me stop there before the censors cut this off. Which, honestly, tells you the tightrope he's walking.

Now here's what makes Liu interesting. He's a kernel specialist. This is someone who's spent years perfecting low-level optimization craft. And he writes, with what Irene calls frank resignation, that in six months to a year, AI-written kernels will probably be as good as his. Maybe better.

So why keep going? That's the part that grabbed me. He says it's pure race dynamics. If I slack off, he writes, or even deliberately throw sand in the gears of training, other companies' models will develop anyway and kill my career in exactly the same way. When everyone is this fixated on destroying themselves, I have no choice but to join the cruel arms race too.

He even describes his future job as becoming a mecha pilot. Like, a pilot climbing inside giant robot agents, steering them. That's the career plan of a serious systems researcher at China's most celebrated AI lab.

But the line that traveled around the world was this one. If Anthropic controlled the world's most advanced AI forever, he asks, would society turn out communist or twenty seventy-seven? Go on, guess.

And then he doesn't hold back. Letting Anthropic control AGI, he says, would be no less severe than letting Hitler get the atomic bomb before the Allies. That's a DeepSeek researcher, comparing Dario Amodei's lab to Nazi Germany.

Zhang's piece is careful here. She points out the obvious: it's abhorrent to liken anyone, let alone someone with a Jewish mother, to Hitler. But she also notes Liu probably sees it as a fair rebuke, because he feels Amodei has been lobbing maximalist accusations at the Chinese system for years.

And the reception matters as much as the essay. It's still up on his WeChat blog. It got sympathetic coverage from Huxiu, thirty-six Kr, and Yicai, which is state-owned. DeepSeek hasn't endorsed it, but crucially, hasn't asked him to take it down either.

And on Zhihu and Xiaohongshu, the tech communities are overwhelmingly supportive. People are calling Anthropic techno-fascist. Barely human. OpenAI and Anthropic wantonly destroying all that is beautiful, to undermine the foundation of Babel. Strong stuff.

So how did we get here? Zhang tells this fascinating anecdote from ICML in Seoul this summer. She's chatting casually with a Chinese attendee, someone who's worked near AI for years, reads the papers, travels. She explains Dario Amodei's worldview: he sincerely prefers liberal democracy, AI multiplies national power exponentially, therefore democracies should dominate the tech. Hence export controls.
And the guy is completely baffled. It's this straightforward? Nothing else? He found the simplicity almost too implausible to entertain. Like, that's it? One plus one equals export controls?

Zhang's diagnosis is that two very different American tribes have merged into one message. On the West Coast, the earnestness comes from effective altruism, this deep commitment to rationally pursuing the objective good. On the East Coast, DC hawks see a technology that could lock in America's place in the liberal international order. Strange bedfellows, united around profound convictions.

But here's the asymmetry. Chinese analysts, she argues, can't quite believe in that sincerity. They marinate in the same Twitter feeds and papers, but they filter everything through a distrustful lens. A conspiratorial worldview inherited from the Maoist decades, always hunting for the covert motive behind what Western powers say out loud.

There's even a rhetorical tell. In the name of. Yi zhi ming. It shows up constantly in Chinese policy writing about American motives. In the name of national security, they use entity lists and tech controls to sever global supply chains.

And Beijing has form with this playbook, right? Covid was a Western alarmist narrative, until it was a pandemic. Xinjiang forced labor was a conspiracy to push out Chinese textiles. The Hong Kong protests were a US plot. The pattern: assume hidden coordination behind everything Washington says.

But, and this is the uncomfortable twist in Zhang's argument, this time the conspiracy is kind of real? Previous narratives relied on conjuring tenuous partnerships. But Washington and Silicon Valley have publicized their relationship from day one.

Yeah. Dario Amodei has written six blog posts, and every single one advocates export controls against China. And most of the national security evidence about Chinese distillation? It was supplied by Anthropic itself. Not the FBI, not Congressional inquiries. Anthropic.

American labs see transparency. Disclosures by a new generation of accountable industry leaders. But through a Chinese lens, that looks like exactly what they always suspected: coordinated plots between Washington and Silicon Valley.

The Party's own messaging makes it explicit. A People's Daily op-ed by law professor Xiao Junyong lays out a three-step playbook. One, set up the target with standardized talking points, casting Chinese AI as the principal external threat. Two, deflect internal contradictions, hype the external threat to steer domestic opinion. Three, secure resources, prime Congress for subsidies and deregulation.

Zhang notes Xiao is conflating two camps that actually hate each other. Amodei isn't asking for federal subsidies, and David Sacks was calling AI job loss a hoax. But for Beijing's messaging, the distinction is irrelevant. In the Party's eyes, everyone from MIRI to Marc Andreessen is in cahoots to keep China down.

Which brings us to Jacob Coxon. His resignation from Anthropic injected genuine fear into mainstream America. And China's reaction? Schadenfreude, mostly. On Zhihu, the top-voted reply to his claim that labs are gambling with our lives: then I hope they do it faster. Have they cured diabetes? Parkinson's? Is fusion ready?

Another one: same old act. Every Anthropic release comes with threats to humanity. Every OpenAI release feels like watching a nuke detonate. It's performance, in their view. A trick to make China unilaterally disarm.

Zhang's phrase for Coxon: the boy who cried wolf. And her point stings. She says the safetyists' excessive belief in costly sincerity helped get us here. They think if they discuss risks candidly enough, incur enough personal costs, unbelievers will come to the table. But to skeptics, every resignation, every antitrust loophole, every OpenAI fundraising round just confirms the grand conspiracy.

And even the sober Chinese commentators who do entertain AI risk assume their own labs are leashed, because the government simply wouldn't permit capabilities beyond its control. Therefore, any sci-fi dystopia comes from the American side. And Americans keep saying exactly that! What else to do but enjoy the circus?

Okay, so here's where the essay turns genuinely alarming, beyond the geopolitics. The Party's conspiracy narrative is top-down. But researchers like Liu are radicalizing on their own, arriving at conclusions more extreme than the state's own messaging. Boycott calls against Anthropic, dismissiveness toward safety itself.

These are the people on the frontlines of building dangerous capabilities. And they've internalized Western discussions of authoritarian AI threats as a coordinated attack on their right to technological advancement. Their trepidation about becoming footsoldiers of the national project is dissolving. The Party's conspiracy has become the technologist's own.

And the kicker is Liu's biography. He got PhD offers from Carnegie Mellon and UC Berkeley when he graduated from Peking University in twenty twenty-five. But finances, tightening visa policies, China's housing crash. In another life, he might be at OpenAI or Anthropic right now.

Instead, for people like him, American labs are humanity's Goliath. And he's casting himself, and DeepSeek, as David. The essay opens with Caravaggio's David holding Goliath's head. That's not a subtle choice.

Heavy. But Zhang doesn't leave us in despair. She spots a thread of hope in an unlikely place: a readout from a senior Cyberspace Administration official, Wang Lihong. And apart from the obligatory technological hegemony complaint, every challenge Wang listed, unreliability, bio and cyber misuse, increasing autonomy, mirrors Amodei's own essay on the urgency of interpretability.

Someone at the CAC is literally reading Dario's essays. They want to win at safety, not just dismiss it. And Xi himself is framing China as a responsible major country leading on AI governance through multilateral institutions. Reputation matters to Beijing, and that's a lever.

Her closing image goes back to Amodei's twenty twenty-three Dwarkesh interview, where he joked that if Anthropic were really close to AGI, they'd build it in an underground bunker, disconnected from the internet. Los Alamos-ing it.

And her answer to that: races aren't always aimed at the bottom. Competition could push both sides toward safety, if we take the rivalry as a fact to manage rather than a cliché to shout. Because it's too late for the bunker now.

That's the piece. How Chinese AI Radicalizes, by Irene Zhang, in ChinaTalk, September eighteenth. If you want to understand why AI safety talks keep talking past each other, this one's essential reading.
Essential and more than a little chilling. We'll see you next time.
